title: Fears AI to 'supercharge surveillance'
full_text:
The Albanese government is resisting bureaucrats' demand for protections from artificial intelligence to be enshrined in enterprise agreements, as agencies ramp up their use of the technology.
The main public sector union wants safeguards to stop agencies from using AI to surveil members as private sector employers around the world roll out technology that closely monitors workers' performance.
"The technology is moving really quickly," Community and Public Sector Union National Secretary Rebecca Fawcett told The Canberra Times in an interview.
"What's not appropriate is AI technology being used to supercharge surveillance technology, so that workers feel like they're being watched every single minute of the day."
With APS-wide bargaining underway, the CPSU has lodged a claim for a common condition to enshrine "firm protections against AI being used for surveillance, performance assessment, recruitment or promotion" - and for "clear human oversight and accountability" to be assured.
Some companies have started using AI to surveil workers, such as by monitoring phone calls or using heat maps to track employees' toilet breaks or monitor their emotional states, in what have been described as "dystopian" uses of the technology.
Ms Fawcett said the CPSU was determined to "lock workplace protections into enterprise agreements to remove that possibility, so workers know that the technology is not going to be used to surveil their work, listen to their calls, take on their performance management and be involved in assessing their conduct and performance."
Such protections were vital to "the trust of the workforce," she said.
Finance and Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher said when announcing the AI Plan for the APS in November that "trust, both from public servants and from the broader public, is our license to operate."
But the government does not support a standalone common condition on AI, arguing that learning and development and consultative committee common conditions would adequately address the issue and provide "a clear expectation that appropriate support is available where AI forms part of an employee's work."
Australian Public Service Commission chief negotiator Alison Stott said this was to avoid embedding "prescriptive or overly detailed provisions" that could risk "becoming quickly outdated, potentially leaving the enterprise agreements misaligned with current practice, community expectations and the broader regulatory landscape."
But Ms Fawcett said this approach was not good enough. "What's on the table in APS-wide bargaining falls well short of the strong, enforceable AI protections workers need, and CPSU members expect," she said.
The union was concerned by the potential for AI decision-making in performance management and workers "should be supported to do their best at work" with coaching and training.
The APSC recently took the unusual step of reminding agencies of their existing obligations in current EBAs to engage in "genuine and effective consultation" with employees on matters that affect them in the workplace.
The commission has confirmed this was intended to guide APS leaders in their adoption of AI.
Ms Fawcett said the circular, which also reminded agencies that the government expected them to be model employers, "sends a good signal to agencies that there are existing consultation obligations that they should be following when it comes to the full range of decisions that affect people at work, including the implementation of AI".
"Our members want to see the APS be a model employer on AI, and we do have that commitment from government," she said. "We want to see that commitment matched by action in this round of bargaining."
Senator Gallagher, who met with Ms Fawcett last week, said the government would "continue to listen and negotiate in good faith" as bargaining continued.
It's understood the Commonwealth response to the union's claim does not address its concerns about surveillance. Also contested is whether employment-related decisions should be required to involve human decision-making, with AI not used to filter, rank, sort or shortlist candidates in recruitment or promotion, or to make decisions about performance assessment.
CPSU members want to retain the ability and responsibility to scrutinise AI-assisted outcomes and automated decision-making processes, so government decisions that affect people's lives are based on independent human judgement.
The union wants to force agencies to engage with staff early on proposed AI deployment and use of automated decision-making.
